sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A smooth curve rising toward a steady level.
sections.body_md:
Feedback linearization rewrites a control-affine plant by an input map. For \(\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x) u\) with \(g(x) \neq 0\), the choice
\[
u = (v - f(x))/g(x)
\]
is an identity: after the substitution, \(\dot{x} = v\) exactly, including far from any equilibrium. It is not the Jacobian. The Jacobian approximates \(f\) near one resting point and leaves a remainder. This cancellation has no remainder on the set where \(g\) stays away from zero.

The new input \(v\) is then designed as an ordinary linear state feedback. The poles you assign are the poles of that exact linear system.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: Solving \(f + g u = v\) for the command gives the display above. With \(v = -k x\) the closed loop is \(\dot{x} = -k x\), so the pole sits at \(-k\), wherever the cancellation was valid. The formula divides by \(g(x)\). A root of \(g\) is not a point you skip. It is a point where this particular law stops being defined, even if the original differential equation is perfectly regular there.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(f = 0.65\), \(g = 0.4\), and a requested derivative \(v = -0.3\). The command is \((-0.3 - 0.65)/0.4 = -0.95/0.4 = -2.375\). Adding \(f\) instead of subtracting it would flip the drift and produce a positive command of the same size. Forgetting to divide by \(0.4\) would report \(-0.95\), which is a derivative gap, not a command. The coefficient \(0.4\) has to stay nonzero for the division to mean anything.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Calling this construction a Jacobian linearization imports the small-ball warning that belongs to the other skill and hides the exact identity. The opposite mistake is to trust the identity on a region where \(g\) changes sign or hits zero. A large outer gain does not shrink the required command. It usually increases the \(v\) you are asking the cancellation to produce, and the actuator may be unable to supply the result. Setting \(g\) to \(1\) by hand invents a plant you do not have.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Where a single cancellation cannot cover the region, a family of linear designs at chosen operating points can be interpolated from a measured schedule. Where the cancelling command would violate an actuator limit, a finite-horizon problem can mark that command illegal and pick a feasible one. Both of those are different architectures. They start from the admission that the identity on this page has a boundary.
